slides.text:
Rust has many integer types. A name is a letter and a number of bits.

- `i` is signed: negatives too
- `u` is unsigned: zero and up
- sizes: 8, 16, 32, 64, 128
slides.code:
let small: i16 = -300;
let huge: u128 = 7;

slides.text:
`isize` and `usize` take the size of the machine: 64 bits on a 64-bit computer.

A number with no type at all becomes an `i32`.

exercises.title: Signed integers
exercises.guide: Declare signed integers of different sizes.

chunks.guide: Signed types hold negative numbers. The number in the name is how many bits the type takes.

notes.text: The type Rust picks when you give none.

chunks.text:
let temperature: i8 = -12;
    let altitude: i32 = -420;

chunks.guide: A number above two billion needs a bigger type.

notes.text: Twice the bits, so it holds huge numbers.

exercises.title: Stock totals
exercises.guide: Add up stock counts and see what is still missing.

chunks.guide: Two small counts fit a u8, and so does their sum.
Orders are bigger, so they get a u32. Both sides of a sum share one type.
A warehouse holds up to 60000 boxes: too many for a u8, so a u16 is the smallest fit.

exercises.title: Pick by range
exercises.guide: `balance` goes from -100 to 100. `stock` goes from 0 to 60000. Give each the smallest type that holds its range.

exercises.title: The smallest fit
exercises.guide: The program prints a screen width. Widths are never negative and stay under 4000. Which is the smallest type that holds any width?
exercises.explanation: `u8` stops at 255 and `i8` at 127, so 3840 does not fit. `u16` reaches 65535. `u32` works too but spends more bits than needed.

slides.text:
A number in code is a literal. You can make it easier to read, give it a type, or write it in another base.

- `_` between digits is ignored
- a suffix after the digits sets the type
- a prefix picks the base: `0x`, `0o` or `0b`

Hex uses the digits 0 to 9 and a to f. Binary uses only 0 and 1. They are plain integers: printing one shows the decimal value.

`b'A'` is the byte value of a letter, typed `u8`. Chars themselves come in a later module.

exercises.title: Underscores in numbers
exercises.guide: Group the digits of big numbers, then compute with them.

chunks.guide: Underscores can go anywhere between digits. The value stays the same.
Printing shows the numbers without them.

exercises.title: Type suffix
exercises.guide: Name the type in the number itself.

chunks.guide: A suffix gives the literal its type, with no annotation on the variable.

notes.text: The suffix makes this number a u8.
An underscore may come before the suffix.

chunks.guide: Three billion does not fit an i32, so the suffix is needed.

exercises.title: Bases and bytes
exercises.guide: Write numbers in other bases, and letters as bytes.

chunks.guide: A prefix picks the base. Hex is common for colors, octal for file permissions.

notes.text: Hexadecimal: digits 0 to 9 and a to f.
Binary: only 0 and 1, grouped for reading.

chunks.guide: `b'A'` is the byte value of a letter, typed u8.

notes.text: The byte value of the letter A.

chunks.text:
println!("{} {} {}", white, perms, mask);
    println!("{} {} {}", upper, lower, gap);

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the literals, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: Printing shows decimal: `0x10` is 16 and `0b11` is 3. The underscore in `1_000` is ignored.

slides.text:
A type of n bits holds 2 to the power n different values.

- unsigned: from 0 up to 2^n - 1
- signed: from -2^(n-1) up to 2^(n-1) - 1

With 8 bits that is 256 values, split between negatives and positives when signed.
Every integer type exposes its limits as constants: `MIN`, `MAX`, and `BITS` for its size. You reach them through the type name. What happens past a limit is a later module.
slides.code:
let top = i64::MAX;
let size = u64::BITS;

exercises.title: MIN and MAX
exercises.guide: Read the smallest and largest value of a type.

chunks.guide: The limits of a type are constants on the type itself.

notes.text: The smallest value this type can hold.
The largest value this type can hold.

chunks.text:
let low = i8::MIN;
    let high = i8::MAX;

chunks.guide: Print the limits of the signed one.
Use them straight in a print. `BITS` is the size of the type.

notes.text: How many bits the type uses.

exercises.title: The top of i16
exercises.guide: Work out the range from the bits, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: 16 bits hold 65536 values. A signed type shares them between negatives and positives, so the top is 2^15 - 1.

exercises.title: Which type tops at 255
exercises.guide: The program must print 255. Choose the type whose largest value that is.

exercises.title: The line that does not fit
exercises.guide: One declaration is rejected by the compiler. Which variable is it?
exercises.explanation: With no type, `people` is an `i32`, which stops at 2147483647, so three billion does not fit. The other values are inside their ranges.
